8 Minecraft Alternatives for Kids That Build More Than Blocks
8 Minecraft Alternatives for Kids That Build More Than Blocks
Arjun Rakesh

TL;DR
 Minecraft can be a great game for kids. It supports building, exploration, planning, and spatial creativity.
 The concern is not Minecraft itself. The concern is when Minecraft becomes the only kind of creative screen time your child gets.
 Minecraft mostly helps kids build worlds. Strong alternatives should help kids build stories, questions, designs, sounds, explanations, and original ideas.
 For kids ages 6 to 10, Taroo is the best Minecraft alternative if you want screen time that still feels playful but develops broader creative skills.
 The best approach is not to ban Minecraft. It is to balance it with apps that stretch different parts of your child’s imagination.
Your child opens Minecraft.
Five minutes later, they are digging a tunnel. Ten minutes later, they are building a house. Thirty minutes later, they are still building the house. The roof is very important. The windows are very important. The secret underground room is, apparently, essential.
And honestly, it is impressive.
Minecraft is not mindless screen time. Kids plan, build, explore, revise, and create. Compared with many noisy, reward-heavy games, Minecraft can feel like one of the “good” options.
So this article is not here to tell you that Minecraft is bad.
It is here to ask a better question:
If your child already loves building in Minecraft, what else could their creativity learn to do?
Because creativity is bigger than blocks.
A child can build a castle. But can they explain the story behind it?
They can design a secret base. But can they solve a mystery?
They can copy a YouTube build. But can they invent their own idea from a prompt?
They can place blocks in the right order. But can they describe what they notice, ask smart questions, make sounds, tell stories, and create in different ways?
That is where Minecraft alternatives can help.
The goal is not to replace Minecraft completely. The goal is to give your child a healthier creative diet.
What Minecraft gets right
Minecraft deserves its reputation.
At its best, Minecraft gives kids something rare: freedom with tools.
There is no single correct path. A child can build a farm, a roller coaster, a castle, a treehouse, a village, a zoo, or a suspiciously complicated lava trap. They choose the goal, break it into steps, and keep improving the result.
That kind of play can support several useful skills.
Spatial thinking
Minecraft asks kids to think in three dimensions. They imagine how a structure will look from the outside, how rooms connect on the inside, and how different shapes fit together.
Planning
A big build requires sequencing. Kids have to decide what comes first, what materials they need, where things go, and how to fix mistakes.
Persistence
Minecraft builds are rarely perfect on the first try. Kids often rebuild, adjust, and experiment until the thing in their head matches the thing on the screen.
Ownership
This may be Minecraft’s biggest strength. Kids feel like the world is theirs. That sense of ownership is powerful, and it is one reason children return to Minecraft again and again.
All of that is real.
The best Minecraft alternatives should not dismiss those strengths. They should build on them.
Where Minecraft can fall short
The limitation of Minecraft is not that it lacks creativity.
The limitation is that it mainly rewards one kind of creativity: building inside a block-based world.
That is valuable, but it is not the whole picture.
A child may spend hours in Minecraft without practicing storytelling, speaking, emotional imagination, critical observation, collaboration, sound-making, flexible thinking, or explaining their ideas clearly.
And if your child mostly follows online tutorials, Minecraft can quietly shift from creation to imitation. They may still be building, but the original thinking is doing less work.
Again, that does not make Minecraft bad. It just means Minecraft should be part of the mix, not the entire mix.
A strong Minecraft alternative should help kids do at least one of these things:
 Create something beyond a structure.
 Explain their thinking.
 Solve open-ended problems.
 Tell stories.
 Practice communication.
 Build confidence in their own ideas.
 Make screen time feel active, not just absorbing.
What to look for in a Minecraft alternative
Before downloading another app, ask three simple questions.
1. Does it create or consume?
A good Minecraft alternative should leave your child with something they made, solved, said, recorded, designed, or imagined.
That “output” matters. It gives parents something to talk about. It also helps kids see themselves as creators, not just players.
2. Does it stretch a different skill?
If Minecraft already gives your child spatial building, look for an app that adds something new: storytelling, logic, design, music, language, emotional thinking, or problem-solving.
The point is not more screen time. The point is more balanced screen time.
3. Is it safe for younger kids?
For ages 6 to 10, be careful with open multiplayer, public chat, and stranger-facing features. The safest options are single-player, parent-guided, or built specifically for children.
The best Minecraft alternatives for kids
1. Taroo
Best for: Kids 6 to 10 who love creating, imagining, solving, and making things their own
Taroo is the best Minecraft alternative if your child loves the creative side of Minecraft, but you want screen time to stretch more than spatial building.
Minecraft asks: “What can you build?”
Taroo asks: “What can you imagine, explain, solve, perform, and create?”
That shift is important.
In Minecraft, a child’s creativity often becomes a structure. In Taroo, creativity can become a story, a question, a sound, a mystery solution, a design, or an explanation.
Taroo is built around playful creative quests. Kids move through a cozy world with different guilds and activities that develop different kinds of creative thinking. They might describe what is happening in an image, solve a silly mystery, ask questions to figure something out, mimic animal sounds, make something with household materials, or explain their choices.
For a Minecraft-loving child, this works because Taroo still respects play. It does not feel like a worksheet. It gives kids a mission, a world, and a reason to use their imagination.
The difference is that Taroo guides the creativity more intentionally.
A child who is great at building houses in Minecraft may discover they are also great at describing scenes in Caption Lab.
A child who loves Redstone contraptions may enjoy solving clues in mystery-style games.
A child who builds animal farms may love Parrot Play, where they mimic sounds like a cat asking for milk or a woodpecker using paper.
A child who enjoys designing rooms may enjoy making, crafting, and explaining what they created.
That breadth is the point.
Minecraft builds one creative muscle very well. Taroo gives kids a creative gym.
Why it is a strong Minecraft alternative:
 It keeps screen time playful and imaginative.
 It helps kids practice storytelling, observation, communication, sound, problem-solving, and making.
 It gives kids creative prompts instead of leaving everything completely open-ended.
 It works especially well for ages 6 to 10.
 It helps parents see what their child is creating and how they are growing.
Possible downside:
Taroo is not a 3D sandbox. If your child wants to build a giant castle block by block, Minecraft is still the better tool for that. Taroo is better when you want broader creative development, not just construction.
2. LEGO Builder’s Journey
Best for: Kids who love calm building and spatial puzzles
LEGO Builder’s Journey is one of the most natural Minecraft alternatives for kids who enjoy building but could use a quieter, more focused experience.
Instead of an endless sandbox, it gives children small LEGO-based puzzles. They place bricks, build paths, and figure out how to move through each scene.
It is beautiful, calm, and thoughtful. For kids who love the building side of Minecraft but get overwhelmed by open-ended worlds, LEGO Builder’s Journey can be a great fit.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Strong spatial reasoning.
 Calm, polished experience.
 Encourages patient problem-solving.
 Feels creative without being chaotic.
Possible downside:
It is not as open-ended as Minecraft. Once a child completes the puzzles, replay value may be lower.
3. Tinkercad
Best for: Kids 8+ who want to build real 3D designs
Tinkercad is a browser-based 3D design tool. It is not a game in the same way Minecraft is, but that is exactly why it can be such a powerful next step.
Minecraft lets kids build with blocks. Tinkercad lets kids design objects more like an engineer, designer, or inventor.
They can create models, combine shapes, experiment with scale, and even export designs for 3D printing if they have access to a printer through school, a library, or a maker space.
For kids who love Minecraft because they like building things, Tinkercad can make that interest feel more real.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Builds real design and engineering habits.
 Great for spatial thinking.
 Free to use.
 Connects digital creativity to physical objects.
Possible downside:
It has a learning curve. Younger kids will likely need adult help at the beginning.
4. Code.org
Best for: Kids who want to understand how games and technology work
Some kids love Minecraft because they enjoy building worlds. Others love it because they want to understand systems.
For those kids, Code.org is a strong alternative.
It teaches coding concepts through visual activities, games, and step-by-step challenges. For kids who are curious about how games work behind the scenes, this can turn screen time into a first step toward programming.
It is especially useful for children who have started asking questions like:
“How do people make games?”
“What is coding?”
“Can I build my own app?”
Why it is a good alternative:
 Free.
 Teaches computational thinking.
 Good for kids who enjoy logic and systems.
 Gives a clearer learning path than open-ended sandbox play.
Possible downside:
It can feel more like learning than play. Some kids will need a parent to sit with them for the first few sessions.
5. Scratch
Best for: Kids who want to make their own games, animations, and stories
Scratch is one of the best creative coding tools for kids.
Instead of just playing a game, children can make their own interactive stories, animations, games, and characters. They drag and connect coding blocks to control what happens on screen.
For a Minecraft fan, Scratch is a useful shift from “I built something inside a game” to “I made a game-like thing myself.”
That is a big creative jump.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Free.
 Excellent for creative coding.
 Lets kids make animations, stories, and games.
 Encourages experimentation and debugging.
Possible downside:
Scratch has a large online community. Younger kids should use it with parent guidance and appropriate privacy settings.
6. DragonBox
Best for: Kids who like patterns, systems, and math puzzles
DragonBox is a set of math games that make concepts like algebra, numbers, and geometry feel more intuitive.
This is not a Minecraft clone. But it can appeal to the same child who likes systems, patterns, and figuring out how things fit together.
Where Minecraft builds spatial plans, DragonBox builds mathematical thinking.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Makes math feel playful.
 Strong for kids who dislike traditional math worksheets.
 Good for ages 5 to 12 depending on the app.
 Encourages logic and pattern recognition.
Possible downside:
It is narrower than Minecraft. It is great for math thinking, but not a general creative world.
7. Animal Crossing: New Horizons
Best for: Kids who want gentle world-building without combat pressure
Animal Crossing is a cozy life-simulation game where kids decorate an island, collect items, catch bugs and fish, and interact with friendly animal neighbors.
It is not as construction-heavy as Minecraft, but it scratches a similar itch: making a world feel like your own.
For younger kids who get stressed by Minecraft survival mode or pulled into endless building sessions, Animal Crossing can feel calmer and more contained.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Gentle and creative.
 Strong design and decorating elements.
 No pressure to win.
 Good for kids who enjoy routine and personalization.
Possible downside:
It requires a Nintendo Switch. Online visits should be limited to trusted friends or family.
8. Procreate or Procreate Dreams
Best for: Kids who are ready to create art, characters, and animations
If your child mostly loves Minecraft because they like making things look a certain way, a visual creation app may be a better alternative than another game.
Procreate lets kids draw, paint, and create digital art. Procreate Dreams adds animation and storytelling possibilities.
This is a different kind of creativity from Minecraft, but a valuable one. Instead of building a world with blocks, kids can design characters, sketch scenes, draw inventions, or animate a story.
Why it is a good alternative:
 Turns screen time into art time.
 Gives kids a real creative output.
 Great for visual thinkers.
 No open-world distractions.
Possible downside:
It works best with an iPad and stylus. Younger kids may need simple prompts to avoid just doodling randomly.
So, what is the best Minecraft alternative?
It depends on what your child loves most about Minecraft.
If they love building, try LEGO Builder’s Journey or Tinkercad.
If they love systems, try Code.org, Scratch, or DragonBox.
If they love decorating and peaceful worlds, try Animal Crossing.
If they love visual design, try Procreate.
But if your child loves Minecraft because they are creative, curious, imaginative, and full of ideas, Taroo is the best next step for ages 6 to 10.
That is because Taroo does not replace creativity with lessons. It expands what creativity can look like.
A Minecraft session might end with a house.
A Taroo session might end with a story, a sound, a solved mystery, a better question, a crafted object, or a new way of explaining what your child sees.
That is a different kind of creative growth.
And for parents, it gives you something Minecraft often does not: a clearer view into how your child thinks.
How to balance Minecraft with creative alternatives
The easiest mistake is to frame this as a punishment.
Do not say:
“You play too much Minecraft. You need to do something educational.”
That turns the alternative into broccoli.
Instead, try:
“You’re already really good at building in Minecraft. Let’s try something that uses a different kind of creativity.”
Or:
“Today, let’s do one building game and one creative challenge.”
A simple weekly rhythm could be:
 Minecraft for open-ended building.
 Taroo for creative quests.
 Code.org or Scratch for coding.
 Procreate for art.
 Animal Crossing or LEGO Builder’s Journey for calm design play.
This makes screen time feel less like a battle and more like a creative menu.
Some days your child builds. Some days they draw. Some days they solve. Some days they tell stories. Some days they make weird animal sounds into a microphone and laugh for five minutes.
That is not wasted time.
That is a child learning that creativity has many forms.
Final thoughts
Minecraft is one of the rare games that many parents are right to respect.
It gives kids room to build, explore, and create. That is worth protecting.
But even a good game can become too narrow if it is the only thing your child wants to do on a screen.
The best Minecraft alternatives do not shame kids for loving Minecraft. They use that love as a bridge.
From blocks to stories.
From buildings to ideas.
From copying a tutorial to making something original.
From “look what I built” to “listen to what I imagined.”
That is the real opportunity.
Not less creativity.
More kinds of creativity.
Frequently asked questions
Is Minecraft good for kids?
Minecraft can be good for kids, especially when used in moderation and with safe settings. It supports building, exploration, spatial thinking, planning, and persistence. The main concern is when it becomes the only kind of creative screen time a child gets.
What is the best Minecraft alternative for kids?
For kids ages 6 to 10, Taroo is the best Minecraft alternative if you want broader creative growth. Minecraft helps kids build worlds. Taroo helps kids tell stories, solve mysteries, describe what they notice, make sounds, ask questions, and create in different ways.
Is Taroo like Minecraft?
Taroo and Minecraft are both creative, playful, and kid-friendly, but they work differently. Minecraft is a 3D sandbox where kids build with blocks. Taroo is a creative quest world where kids practice storytelling, observation, communication, problem-solving, sound, and making.
What is a good free Minecraft alternative?
Code.org, Scratch, and Tinkercad are strong free options. Code.org is best for coding basics, Scratch is best for making games and animations, and Tinkercad is best for 3D design. Younger kids may need adult guidance with all three.
What age is Minecraft best for?
Minecraft is often best for older elementary kids and up, especially when parents manage online settings. Younger kids can enjoy creative mode, but they may need help staying safe, avoiding open multiplayer, and balancing Minecraft with other activities.
Should I delete Minecraft?
Not necessarily. Minecraft can be part of a healthy screen-time mix. Instead of deleting it, try balancing it with apps that stretch other creative skills. For example, use Minecraft for building, Taroo for creative quests, Scratch for coding, and Procreate for art.
What skills does Minecraft build?
Minecraft can support spatial reasoning, planning, persistence, and open-ended building. It is less intentional about storytelling, communication, emotional thinking, language, and guided creative problem-solving. That is why many parents look for alternatives that build a broader range of skills.
How do I get my child to try something other than Minecraft?
Do not present the new app as a punishment. Connect it to what they already love. Try saying, “You’re great at building in Minecraft. Let’s try a game that uses your creativity in a different way.” Start with short sessions and let them choose the activity that feels most fun.

Apps Like Pinterest for Kids: Safer Ways to Find Creative Ideas
Apps Like Pinterest for Kids: Safer Ways to Find Creative Ideas
Bhaskar Samineni

Apps Like Pinterest for Kids: Safer Ways to Find Creative Ideas
TL;DR
Pinterest is excellent at one thing: putting interesting ideas in front of you.
But it is not designed for younger children. Pinterest requires users to be at least 13, and for kids below that age, parents may want something that offers creative inspiration inside a more age-appropriate experience.
The best alternative depends on where your child gets inspired.
Some kids need a prompt: What should I make?
Some are inspired by other children: What did someone else do with this idea?
Others already know what they like and want to explore: Show me more drawing ideas, LEGO builds, crafts, or animals.
For kids who need inspiration and somewhere to turn it into something of their own, Taroo is our top pick. Kids can choose from a large library of creative quests across stories, drawing, music, speaking, and observation, take part in weekly challenges inspired by other kids' creations, and use AI as a co-creator to develop and improve their ideas.
Other good options include LEGO Play for kid-safe building inspiration, Scratch for projects made by other young creators, Crayola Create & Play for art-focused prompts, DIY.org for creative challenges, Zigazoo for peer inspiration, and YouTube Kids for exploring specific interests.
Short answer: what should kids use instead of Pinterest?
Start with the kind of inspiration your child needs.
| If your child is thinking… | Type of inspiration |  |
 --- 
| “I don't know what to make.” | Prompt-led inspiration | Taroo, Crayola Create & Play, DIY.org |
| “Show me what other kids made.” | Peer-led inspiration | Taroo Weekly Challenges, LEGO Play, Scratch, Zigazoo |
| “I already know what I like. Show me more.” | Interest-led inspiration | YouTube Kids, LEGO Play, Crayola Create & Play |
The categories overlap. That is useful.
A child might discover a drawing idea through a Taroo quest, see how other kids approached the weekly challenge, then use AI feedback to take their own version further.
The goal is not simply to give kids more things to scroll through.
It is to shorten the distance between “that's cool” and “I made this.”
Why parents look for Pinterest alternatives for kids
Pinterest can be a wonderful creativity engine.
Search for “cardboard castle,” “dragon drawing,” or “Minecraft house,” and you can find hundreds of possible directions within seconds.
For adults, that freedom works well. We usually know why we opened Pinterest, what we are looking for, and roughly what we plan to do afterward.
Kids often need more structure.
A child can start by looking for a drawing idea and end up browsing bedroom designs, birthday cakes, costumes, crafts, and dozens of unrelated images without ever beginning the original drawing.
That does not make Pinterest bad. Discovery and serendipity are part of its appeal.
But there are two practical problems for younger children.
First, Pinterest is not intended for users under 13.
Second, finding inspiration is not the same as creating.
Children often benefit from a clearer starting point, a bounded set of possibilities, and something that helps them continue once the first idea arrives.
That is what the best Pinterest alternatives for kids should provide.
What to look for in a Pinterest alternative
1. Does it actually spark ideas?
A creative app should expose children to possibilities they may not have thought of themselves.
That could come from a challenge, another child's creation, a themed activity, or a library of interesting content.
2. Is discovery age-appropriate?
A child should not need to navigate an adult social platform just to find an idea for something to draw.
Look for moderated content, parental controls, age-appropriate interaction, and clear limits around social features.
3. Does inspiration lead to action?
This is the biggest one.
After ten minutes, did your child only see ideas?
Or did they begin drawing, building, writing, recording, designing, or experimenting?
4. Does the child still make the creative decisions?
Examples can inspire children, but they can also turn into copying.
The best creative experiences leave enough space for the child to decide:
What would mine look like?
What would I change?
What happens next?
Can I make this funnier, stranger, louder, or more interesting?
Best apps for prompt-led inspiration
These are best for the moment when a child wants to create but has no idea where to begin.
1. Taroo
Best for: Kids who want an idea and somewhere to take it
Taroo starts with a different assumption from Pinterest.
A child should not need to know what to search for before they can be creative.
Instead, kids can choose from a growing library of creative quests across drawing, storytelling, music, speaking, observation, and other forms of making.
One quest might ask them to imagine what is happening in an unusual picture. Another might start a story they need to continue. Another might ask them to create a rhythm, photograph something around them, invent a character, or respond to a drawing challenge.
The quest provides the spark.
The child decides what happens next.
AI then acts as a co-creator. It can react to what the child made, offer feedback, introduce another possibility, or help develop an idea without simply generating the whole finished answer.
That creates a useful loop:
Choose a challenge → make something → get a response → change it → keep creating
Taroo also adds a second source of inspiration through weekly challenges. Kids can work from a shared creative starting point and see the different directions other children take.
Seeing ten polished Pinterest images tells a child what something can look like.
Seeing ten kids respond differently to the same challenge teaches something else:
There is more than one good idea.
Why parents may like it:
 Kids do not need to formulate searches or prompts
 Inspiration covers multiple creative mediums
 The child moves quickly from browsing to making
 Weekly challenges introduce bounded peer inspiration
 AI can help kids iterate rather than simply produce an answer
 The experience is built around creation rather than an endless content feed
Possible downside:
Taroo is not designed for searching a huge visual archive. If your child specifically wants hundreds of reference photos of dinosaurs, hairstyles, bedrooms, or crafts, a discovery platform will provide more breadth.
2. Crayola Create & Play
Best for: Younger kids who want art-focused creative starting points
Crayola Create & Play gives children a broad collection of drawing, coloring, design, and STEAM activities.
Instead of opening an empty canvas and asking the child to invent everything, the app provides themes and activities such as pixel art, coloring pages, rocket crafting, shapes, and other creative tasks. Crayola says new activities and creative quests are added regularly, and the app is designed around age-appropriate creative development.
This makes it especially useful for younger children who enjoy art but often say, “I don't know what to draw.”
Why parents may like it:
 Strong focus on drawing and visual creativity
 Lots of built-in starting points
 Designed specifically for children
 Mixes creativity with simple STEAM activities
Possible downside:
The creative range is narrower than Taroo. It is strongest for visual art and younger children rather than storytelling, speaking, music, or broader creative expression.
3. DIY.org
Best for: Kids who like projects and making things
DIY.org is built around the idea that children learn through making. Its current platform includes creative challenges, tools for making games and digital projects, and a community where children can share what they create. DIY says its experience is designed for ages 5–15, with moderated communities, no ads, and parent controls.
For children who like a clear challenge and a project to complete, that can be much more actionable than scrolling through visual inspiration.
Why parents may like it:
 Project-based rather than purely consumptive
 Challenges provide clear starting points
 Children can make and share finished projects
 Designed around a younger audience
Possible downside:
Its current emphasis increasingly includes digital making and AI-assisted game creation, so it may not suit a child simply looking for casual drawing or craft inspiration.
Best apps for inspiration from other kids
Children do not only get ideas from adults, experts, or polished examples.
Sometimes the most motivating thing is seeing what another child imagined.
Peer inspiration can make creativity feel more attainable: Someone my age made that. What could I make?
It also needs more careful safety design because sharing creations introduces social features.
1. Taroo Weekly Challenges
Taroo's weekly challenges are designed around a bounded version of peer inspiration.
Children begin from the same creative challenge, make their own version, and can discover how differently other kids interpreted it.
The important part is the shared starting point.
If one challenge asks children to invent a strange character, one child might make a nervous alien, another a talking sandwich, and another a superhero pigeon.
The value is not finding the “best” answer.
It is seeing the range of possible answers and getting ideas for your own.
This complements Taroo's quest library well: quests provide prompt-led inspiration, while challenges provide peer-led inspiration.
2. LEGO Play
Best for: Kids inspired by other builders
LEGO Play is unusually close to a kid-friendly Pinterest experience within one specific creative interest.
Children can share photos of their LEGO creations, browse a social feed for inspiration, watch videos, and make digital creations. LEGO says posts, usernames, hashtags, and comments are moderated before appearing, children cannot directly message one another, and human faces are not allowed in shared photos.
For a child who already loves building, that creates a simple loop:
See a build → get an idea → build something → share it
Why parents may like it:
 Inspiration comes from other LEGO creators
 Community is built specifically around kids
 Posts and interactions are moderated
 No direct messaging
 Free to use
Possible downside:
It is obviously LEGO-specific. A child looking for stories, music, drawing, photography, or broader creative ideas will hit the boundaries quickly.
3. Scratch
Best for: Kids inspired by games, animations, and interactive projects
Scratch combines a creation tool with a huge community of projects made by other users.
Children can explore games, animations, stories, and experiments, then make or remix projects of their own. Scratch is primarily designed for ages 8–16 and is maintained by the MIT Media Lab's Lifelong Kindergarten group.
This makes it particularly powerful for kids who learn by seeing something interesting and wondering:
How did they make that?
Why parents may like it:
 Children can move directly from viewing to creating
 Strong for coding, games, and animation
 Projects provide concrete examples of what is possible
 Can grow significantly in complexity with the child
Possible downside:
Scratch is a public online community. Younger children need parent involvement, and its creative scope is primarily interactive digital projects rather than every kind of creative activity.
Best apps for exploring an interest
Sometimes a child does not need help deciding whether to create.
They already know exactly what they are interested in.
They want:
“Dragon drawing ideas.”
“Cool LEGO spaceships.”
“Things I can make with cardboard.”
“Easy piano songs.”
“Minecraft castles.”
That is where Pinterest's model is strongest: start with an interest and explore outward.
For younger kids, these alternatives can provide a more appropriate version of that behavior.
1. YouTube Kids
Best for: Broad interest-led discovery
YouTube Kids gives children access to a much broader range of topics than most dedicated creativity apps.
A child interested in drawing dinosaurs, simple crafts, music, science experiments, building, origami, or animation can find videos around that interest.
Parents can adjust content settings, disable search, block channels, set timers, or use an “Approved content only” mode where children can only access videos and collections chosen by the parent. YouTube itself notes that its filtering systems are not perfect, so parent judgment still matters.
Why parents may like it:
 Extremely broad range of interests
 Easy for kids to follow a curiosity
 Strong parental controls
 Useful for visual inspiration
Possible downside:
It is primarily a viewing platform. A child can easily spend the entire session consuming inspiration without creating anything afterward.
2. LEGO Play
Best for: Kids whose interest is building
LEGO Play also works well here because its discovery feed is focused.
Instead of searching the entire internet for building inspiration, kids explore LEGO creations, videos, and challenges inside an environment designed around one interest. LEGO describes the app as a place where children can explore a moderated social feed specifically to find inspiration for their next creation.
That narrowness is a limitation if your child has many interests.
But if the interest is LEGO, it is also the product's greatest advantage.
3. Crayola Create & Play
Best for: Kids whose interest is drawing, coloring, and visual art
For children who already know they want to make art, Crayola Create & Play provides a more bounded place to explore.
Kids can move between coloring, pixel art, drawing, themed creative activities, design, and simple STEAM experiences without navigating an open web search.
It does not have Pinterest's enormous variety.
For a six-year-old who mainly wants art ideas, that may be a feature rather than a problem.
So, what is the best Pinterest alternative for kids?
It depends on what happens immediately before your child says, “I'm bored.”
If they want to make something but do not know what, try Taroo, Crayola Create & Play, or DIY.org.
If they get excited by seeing what other kids made, try Taroo's Weekly Challenges, LEGO Play, Scratch, or Zigazoo.
If they already have a strong interest and want more ideas around it, YouTube Kids, LEGO Play, or Crayola Create & Play can work well.
But if you want one app that tries to connect the whole creative process — find an idea, make something, see other possibilities, get feedback, and keep improving — Taroo is the strongest fit for kids ages 6–10.
Pinterest is designed to help you discover things worth saving.
Taroo is designed to help a child discover something worth making.
A simple way to stop inspiration from becoming scrolling
Whatever app you choose, one small rule can change the experience:
Pick one idea before finding the next one.
A child does not need to recreate it exactly.
Ask:
 What would you change?
 Can you make your own version?
 What happens next?
 Can you combine this with another idea?
 What would make it sillier?
 Can you turn it into a story?
 Could you build it?
 What would its soundtrack sound like?
The goal is to teach children that inspiration is the beginning of creativity, not the activity itself.
A useful screen-time pattern is:
Discover → choose → create → share
rather than:
Discover → discover → discover → discover.
The takeaway
Pinterest is powerful because it makes possibilities visible.
But younger children do not necessarily need an infinite wall of possibilities.
Sometimes they need one interesting challenge.
Sometimes they need to see another child's idea.
Sometimes they need room to follow an interest they already love.
And once inspiration arrives, they need somewhere to take it.
The best creative apps for kids do not only answer:
“What could I make?”
They help children reach the much more satisfying sentence:
“Look what I made.”
Frequently asked questions
Is Pinterest safe for kids?
Pinterest requires users to be at least 13 years old, with higher minimum ages in some countries. It therefore is not intended as an account-based platform for younger children. Parents can still browse Pinterest themselves and use ideas together with a child.
What is the best Pinterest alternative for a 6-year-old?
For younger kids who need creative starting points, Taroo and Crayola Create & Play are strong choices. LEGO Play can work well for children interested in building. YouTube Kids can also provide interest-led inspiration when parents use its content and search controls.
What is the best Pinterest alternative for an 8-year-old?
Taroo, Scratch, LEGO Play, DIY.org, and YouTube Kids all offer different kinds of inspiration for an 8-year-old. Taroo is strongest for broader guided creativity, Scratch for games and animations, LEGO Play for building, and YouTube Kids for exploring specific interests.
What is the best app for kids to get creative ideas?
Taroo is a strong choice when the child wants ideas they can immediately act on. Its creative quests provide starting points across multiple mediums, while weekly challenges add inspiration from how other kids respond.
Is Taroo like Pinterest?
Not exactly. Pinterest is primarily a discovery platform. Taroo combines inspiration with creation. Children choose creative quests, make their own responses, use AI to develop and iterate on ideas, and can get inspiration from other kids through weekly challenges.
Are there kid-friendly apps where children can see other kids' creations?
Yes. LEGO Play offers a moderated feed of LEGO creations, Scratch lets children explore projects from its programming community, and Zigazoo centers on moderated kid-created video content. Taroo's weekly challenges provide a more bounded version where children see different responses to shared creative prompts.
Is YouTube Kids a good Pinterest alternative?
It can be useful for interest-led inspiration because children can explore drawing, crafts, building, music, and many other interests. It is still primarily a video-viewing platform, so parents may want to pair browsing with a rule that the child chooses something to make afterward. YouTube Kids provides search, content, blocking, and timer controls for parents.
How can I help my child use inspiration without simply copying?
Ask them to change one meaningful thing. Change the character, purpose, material, ending, color, environment, rule, or story behind the idea. The goal is not avoiding influence — all creators use references. The goal is getting the child to make choices of their own.

Best Design Apps for Kids Who Like Making Things
Best Design Apps for Kids Who Like Making Things
Bhaskar Samineni

TL;DR
The best design apps for kids do more than give them a blank canvas. They help children turn an idea into something they can see, play with, improve, and explain.
This list includes apps for different kinds of young makers: Taroo for guided creative projects, Tinkercad for 3D inventions, Canva Education for visual design, Bloxels and Scratch for games, Planner 5D for spaces, Minecraft Creative for worlds, and SketchUp for more advanced 3D design.
If your child is always inventing characters, rearranging rooms, building worlds, drawing objects, or asking “what if I made…?”, these are good places to start.
Short answer: what are the best design apps for kids?
Some of the best design apps for kids include Taroo, Tinkercad, Canva Education, Bloxels, Scratch, Planner 5D, Minecraft Creative, and SketchUp for Schools.
Each supports a different kind of design. Taroo is strongest for kids who need creative starting points and want to make across several mediums. Tinkercad and SketchUp focus on 3D design. Canva focuses on visual communication. Bloxels and Scratch help kids design games and interactive experiences. Planner 5D is useful for rooms and interiors, while Minecraft lets children design entire worlds.
Kids design things all the time.
A cardboard box becomes a spaceship. A bedroom gets rearranged five times. A doodle gets a name, a personality, and suddenly an entire story. A Minecraft house turns into a village.
They may not call any of this “design.”
But the process is already there: imagine something, make choices, see what happens, and change it until it feels right.
A good design app gives kids more ways to practice that process.
Not just prettier output.
More decisions.
What makes a good design app for kids?
The best design apps give children enough structure to start, but enough freedom to make the result their own.
| Design strength | What it looks like |
 --- |
| Ideation | Prompts, challenges, or tools that help kids decide what to make |
| Making | Turning an idea into a story, object, room, game, image, or world |
| Choice | Kids decide how the creation looks, behaves, or develops |
| Iteration | Easy ways to change, test, rebuild, or improve |
| Problem-solving | Working within space, logic, materials, rules, or other constraints |
| Ownership | A finished creation kids can explain or show someone |
The key test is simple:
Did the child make meaningful decisions?
A polished result made mostly by a template is less interesting than a rough result the child genuinely designed.
1. Taroo
Best for: Kids who want creative direction without being told exactly what to make  
Creative focus: Drawing, stories, characters, music, speaking, observation, AI co-creation  
Good fit for: Kids ages 6–10 who have lots of ideas but benefit from a starting point
Taroo approaches design differently from most tools on this list.
Instead of opening with an empty canvas, kids choose from creative quests. They might invent a character, respond to an unusual image, continue a story, create a rhythm, draw something from a prompt, or explore something around them.
The quest gives them somewhere to begin. The child decides where it goes.
AI can respond to their creation, suggest another direction, or help them develop an idea without simply making the finished project for them.
That makes Taroo useful for practicing the part of design that comes before mastering professional tools: deciding what should exist, what makes it interesting, and what should change next.
Why it stands out: It treats design as creative decision-making across many mediums, not just manipulating shapes on a screen.
2. Tinkercad
Best for: Kids who want to invent and design 3D objects  
Creative focus: 3D modeling, spatial design, circuits, simple coding  
Good fit for: Kids interested in inventions, products, buildings, or 3D printing
Tinkercad makes 3D design approachable by reducing objects to simple shapes.
Kids can combine cubes, cylinders, letters, holes, and other forms to build rockets, houses, creatures, furniture, vehicles, keychains, and inventions.
The interesting part is the constraint. An idea has to become dimensions, proportions, and pieces that actually fit together.
For kids who love building things physically, it can be a good first step into digital product design.
Why it stands out: It introduces real 3D-design thinking without starting with professional CAD complexity.
3. Canva Education
Best for: Kids who want to design something other people will see  
Creative focus: Posters, presentations, videos, infographics, layouts  
Good fit for: Kids interested in visual communication and school projects
Canva teaches a form of design children encounter everywhere: arranging words and images so an idea is clear.
Kids can make posters, presentations, invitations, simple videos, infographics, and other visual projects.
Templates make starting easy, but the most useful experience comes when kids begin changing them: deciding what deserves attention, what should be removed, where something belongs, and how the whole page should feel.
Why it stands out: It helps kids understand that design is not only decoration. It is communication.
4. Bloxels
Best for: Kids who want to design a video game without learning code first  
Creative focus: Games, pixel art, characters, levels, storytelling  
Good fit for: Kids who spend a lot of time playing games and want to make one
Bloxels lets children design characters, backgrounds, levels, obstacles, and stories and turn them into playable games.
That introduces a useful new design question:
What will someone else experience?
A level can look beautiful but still be boring. A jump can be too easy. An obstacle can be frustrating. Kids begin thinking about difficulty, pacing, rewards, and player behavior.
Why it stands out: It turns game-playing instincts into game-design decisions.
5. Scratch
Best for: Kids who want more control over games and interactive creations  
Creative focus: Coding, games, animations, interactive stories  
Good fit for: Kids ready to think about logic and behavior
Scratch uses visual code blocks to let kids decide how characters and objects behave.
A child can make something move when clicked, trigger a sound, change scenes, keep score, react to another character, or create rules for an entire game.
Compared with Bloxels, the learning curve is higher. But the creative ceiling is also much higher.
Kids are not only designing what something looks like. They are designing what happens.
Why it stands out: It connects creative expression with logic, systems, and cause and effect.
6. Planner 5D
Best for: Kids who constantly imagine rooms and houses  
Creative focus: Interior design, floor plans, furniture, spatial planning  
Good fit for: Kids interested in architecture, interiors, or rearranging spaces
Planner 5D lets kids lay out rooms, place furniture, experiment with materials, and move between 2D plans and 3D views.
Unlike an unrestricted drawing, space creates real constraints.
Does the couch fit? Where does the door open? Is there enough room to walk through? What happens when the bed moves to the other wall?
Those limitations are part of what makes design interesting.
Why it stands out: It makes kids balance imagination with real spatial constraints.
7. Minecraft Creative
Best for: Kids who want to design entire worlds  
Creative focus: Architecture, landscapes, environments, systems, world-building  
Good fit for: Kids who naturally think bigger than one object
Minecraft Creative removes most resource constraints and lets children focus on building.
A house can become a street. A street can become a town. The town can get roads, farms, parks, underground tunnels, landmarks, and its own visual rules.
That scale makes Minecraft surprisingly rich as a design environment.
The challenge is that complete freedom can also become aimless wandering. Giving kids a project — design a floating village, an animal sanctuary, or a city without cars — can make the experience much stronger.
Why it stands out: Few kid-friendly tools give children this much space to design environments and worlds.
8. SketchUp for Schools
Best for: Older kids ready for more serious architecture and 3D modeling  
Creative focus: Buildings, structures, spatial design, precise 3D models  
Good fit for: Kids whose interest in architecture or design is becoming more serious
SketchUp for Schools is closer to the kind of tool an actual designer might use.
Children can create more precise 3D structures, think about scale and geometry, and gradually move from playful building toward architectural modeling.
It is probably too much tool for many younger children. But for an older kid who has already spent years building in Minecraft or experimenting with Tinkercad, that complexity can be exactly the point.
Why it stands out: It gives serious young builders somewhere to grow.
How to choose the right design app
The best app is not necessarily the most powerful one.
It is the one that matches what your child naturally tries to make.
If your child has lots of ideas but struggles to start, try Taroo.
If they constantly invent objects and gadgets, try Tinkercad.
If they love posters, typography, and visual layouts, try Canva Education.
If they love playing games, try Bloxels first and Scratch when they want more control.
If they constantly redesign bedrooms and houses, try Planner 5D.
If they build cities and worlds, Minecraft Creative is difficult to beat.
If an older child is becoming genuinely interested in architecture or 3D design, try SketchUp.
Before choosing, ask:
 What does my child already make when nobody tells them what to do?
 Does this app give them choices or mostly templates?
 Can they change and improve what they make?
 Will they finish with something they can explain?
 Is the difficulty appropriate enough that the tool does not become the whole challenge?
Where Taroo fits
Professional design tools become powerful once a child already has an idea.
Taroo focuses more on helping that idea emerge and develop.
Kids get creative quests across several mediums, make their own choices, and can co-create with AI when they need another possibility or feedback on where to go next.
It is not a replacement for Tinkercad, Scratch, Minecraft, or Canva.
A child might invent a character in Taroo, build its world in Minecraft, make its game in Scratch, or design an object from that world in Tinkercad.
The tools can build on one another.
The takeaway
Good design apps do not just help kids make polished things.
They give children practice deciding what should exist.
A room needs a layout. A game needs rules. A poster needs hierarchy. A character needs choices. A world needs structure. An invention needs to work.
Then something inevitably does not feel right.
So the child changes it.
That loop — imagine, make, look, change — is the part worth practicing.
Not because every child needs to become a designer.
Because learning to turn an idea into something real is useful almost everywhere.
Frequently asked questions
What is the best design app for kids?
Taroo is a strong choice for broad guided creativity. Tinkercad is excellent for 3D objects, Scratch for interactive projects, Canva for visual design, and Minecraft Creative for world-building.
What is the best free design app for kids?
Scratch and Tinkercad are two strong free options. Scratch focuses on games and interactive experiences, while Tinkercad focuses on 3D objects and inventions.
What is the best design app for a 7-year-old?
Taroo is a good starting point for broad creativity. Depending on the child's interests, Minecraft Creative, Bloxels, or Tinkercad with some adult help can also work well.
What is the best app for kids interested in architecture?
Planner 5D is an approachable starting point for rooms and layouts. Tinkercad works well for simple structures. Older children ready for more precision can move toward SketchUp for Schools.
Do kids need to learn professional design software?
No. Younger children benefit more from making lots of things than mastering complicated software early. As their interests become clearer, more specialized tools can give them greater control.
